questions.question: Which specific ensemble is introduced for classical systems that are isolated from their surroundings?
questions.referenceAnswer: The microcanonical ensemble is defined for a closed classical system.
goldText: In this chapter we develop the foundations of equilibrium statistical mechanics. No attempt will be made to derive the equilibrium theory from the detailed microscopic dynamics. Instead, we will content ourselves with postulating the statistical laws. In Section 2.1 we consider a closed classical system and develop the concept of the microcanonical ensemble. We define the entropy in the thermodynamic limit, and make contact with thermodynamics. In Section 2.2 we extend the formalism to systems in thermal contact with the surroundings and introduce the canonical ensemble. We also discuss fluctuations of thermodynamic variables. The grand canonical ensemble is discussed in Section 2.3 for systems that are free to exchange particles with the outside, and we demonstrate the general relation between fluctuations in particle number and the compressibility. In Section 2.4 we modify the formalism to include quantum systems and introduce the density matrix. An alternative information-theoretic approach is discussed in Section 2.5 and a number of useful thermodynamic variational principles are introduced in Section 2.6.

questions.question: Under what conditions can mixing occur in a physical system?
questions.referenceAnswer: Mixing occurs when an initial compact distribution of points distorts into a convoluted object that permeates the entire surface while maintaining the same volume, a phenomenon proven for systems like hard spheres. In truly isolated systems, mixing is irrelevant, but small amounts of noise in imperfectly insulated systems can distort trajectories sufficiently to effectively produce mixing.
goldText: A hypothesis that leads to statistical mechanics, as we know it, is the mixing hypothesis. Briefly stated, mixing refers to the notion that an initial (compact) distribution of points on T{E) very quickly distorts into a convoluted object which permeates the entire surface while still occupying the same volume (as required by Liouville's theorem). Mixing can be proven to occur, for example, for systems of hard spheres [274] [275]. When one talks about a distribution of points on T(E), one is no longer discussing a single system, and for a truly isolated system, mixing is of course irrelevant. However, the sensitivity of x(i) to minute changes in initial conditions, will allow small amounts of noise in an imperfectly insulated system to distort the trajectory sufficiently that in effect one obtains mixing.

questions.question: What distinguishes a reversible process from an irreversible one regarding the ability to retrace the thermodynamic path?
questions.referenceAnswer: A reversible process follows a path that can be exactly reversed, whereas an irreversible process does not follow the same path when reversed, even if the system returns to its initial state.
goldText:
Before going on to discuss the second law, we pause to introduce some terminology. A thermodynamic transformation or process is any change in the state variables of the system. A spontaneous process is one that takes place without any change in the external constraints on the system, and is due simply to the internal dynamics. An adiabatic process is one in which no heat is exchanged between the system and its surroundings. A process is isothermal if the temperature is held fixed, isobaric if the pressure is fixed, isochoric if the density is constant, and quasistatic if the process is infinitely slow. A reversible process is by nature quasistatic and follows a path in thermodynamic space which can be exactly reversed. If this is not possible, the process is irreversible. An example of a reversible process is the slow adiabatic expansion of a gas against a piston on which a force is exerted externally. This force is infmitesimally less than PA, where P is the pressure of the gas and A the area of the piston. An example of an irreversible process is the free adiabatic expansion of a gas into a vacuum. In this case the initial state of the gas can be recovered if one compresses it and removes excess heat. This is, however, not the same thermodynamic path.

questions.question: How are thermodynamic variables defined for a magnetic solid?
questions.referenceAnswer: For a magnetic solid, the appropriate thermodynamic variables are the magnetic field H, the magnetization M, and the temperature T.
goldText: A macroscopic system has many degrees of freedom, only a few of which are measurable. Thermodynamics thus concerns itself with the relation between a small number of variables which are sufficient to describe the bulk behavior of the system in question. In the case of a gas or liquid the appropriate variables are the pressure P, volume V, and temperature T. In the case of a magnetic solid the appropriate variables are the magnetic field H, the magnetization M, and the temperature T. In more complicated situations, such as when a liquid is in contact with its vapor, additional variables may be needed: such as the volume of both liquid and gas VL, VG, the interfacial area A, and surface tension a. If the thermodynamic variables are independent of time, the system is said to be in a steady state. If, moreover, there are no macroscopic currents in the system, such as a flow of heat or particles through the material, the system is in equilibrium. Any quantity which, in equilibrium, depends only on the thermodynamic variables, rather than on the history of the sample, is called a state function. In subsequent sections we shall meet a number of such quantities. For a large system, the state variables can normally be taken to be either extensive (i.e., proportional to the size of the system) or intensive (i.e., independent of system size).

questions.question: How can the principle of minimizing thermodynamic potentials, which connects the microcanonical and canonical ensembles for classical systems, be extended to determine equilibrium states in quantum systems using the density matrix formalism?
questions.referenceAnswer: The principle that an equilibrium state minimizes a specific free energy applies to closed classical systems at fixed temperature and volume (minimizing Helmholtz free energy) and to systems at constant pressure and temperature (minimizing Gibbs free energy). This variational approach is consistent with results derived from maximum-likelihood arguments for canonical ensembles and information-theoretic arguments involving the density matrix for quantum systems.
goldText: We saw in Section 1.3 that the thermodynamic equilibrium state of a system at fixed temperature and volume is the one that minimizes the Helmholtz free energy. The same result followed from maximum-likelihood arguments in Section 2.2 and from the information-theoretic argument of Section 2.5. Similarly, at equilibrium at constant pressure and temperature the Gibbs free energy is at a minimum. These results can be used in statistical calculations. A common approach is to find an approximate expression for the appropriate free energy in terms of certain parameters, and then to determine the equilibrium values of these parameters by minimizing the free energy. This method will be used frequently in our treatment of phase transitions in Chapter 3. At this point we present a simple example that makes use of this method.

In this chapter we develop the foundations of equilibrium statistical mechanics. No attempt will be made to derive the equilibrium theory from the detailed microscopic dynamics. Instead, we will content ourselves with postulating the statistical laws. In Section 2.1 we consider a closed classical system and develop the concept of the microcanonical ensemble. We define the entropy in the thermodynamic limit, and make contact with thermodynamics. In Section 2.2 we extend the formalism to systems in thermal contact with the surroundings and introduce the canonical ensemble. We also discuss fluctuations of thermodynamic variables. The grand canonical ensemble is discussed in Section 2.3 for systems that are free to exchange particles with the outside, and we demonstrate the general relation between fluctuations in particle number and the compressibility. In Section 2.4 we modify the formalism to include quantum systems and introduce the density matrix. An alternative information-theoretic approach is discussed in Section 2.5 and a number of useful thermodynamic variational principles are introduced in Section 2.6.

This chapter presents a brief review of elementary thermodynamics. It complements Chapter 2, in which the connection between thermodynamics and statistical mechanical ensembles is established. The reader may wish to use this chapter as a short refresher course and may wish to consult one of the many books on thermodynamics, such as that of Callen [55] or Chapters 2 to 4 of the book by Reichl [254], for a more complete discussion of the material. The outline of the present chapter is as follows. In Section 1.1 we introduce the notion of state variables and equations of state. Section 1.2 contains a discussion of the laws of thermodynamics, definition of thermodynamic processes, and the introduction of entropy. In Section 1.3 we introduce the thermodynamic potentials that are most useful from a statistical point of view. The Gibbs-Duhem equation and a number of useful Maxwell relations are derived in Section 1.4. In Section 1.5 we turn to the response functions, such as the specific heat, susceptibility, and compressibility, which provide the common experimental probes of macroscopic systems. Section 1.6 contains a discussion of some general conditions of equilibrium and stability. We discuss the issue of magnetic work in Section 1.7 and we conclude, in 1.8, with a brief discussion of the thermodynamics of phase transitions and the Gibbs phase rule.

questions.question: When a small system exchanges energy and volume with a large reservoir characterized by temperature T0 and pressure P0, how does the condition that its Gibbs potential is minimized relate to the entropy maximization principle used when two isolated systems reach mechanical and thermal equilibrium?
questions.referenceAnswer: The minimization of the Gibbs potential for the small system in contact with a reservoir is mathematically equivalent to maximizing the total entropy of the combined system (small system plus reservoir). Since the reservoir is large, its temperature and pressure remain constant, and the condition for the small system's equilibrium corresponds to the state where the generalized forces (temperature and pressure) are equalized between the subsystem and the reservoir, consistent with the requirement that all conjugate forces must be equal in equilibrium.

questions.referenceAnswer: The unique functional form is derived by requiring that the uncertainty of a composite system be the sum of the uncertainties of its independent subsystems, which leads to S being an extensive variable. However, a rigorous proof for this behavior under general conditions is lacking because real systems are non-integrable and large, unlike trivial examples where equations of motion are integrable.

questions.question: How does the text resolve the apparent contradiction between thermodynamic stability requirements and the existence of materials with negative magnetic susceptibility?
questions.referenceAnswer: The initial definition of the Gibbs potential leads to a requirement that magnetic susceptibility must be positive for thermodynamic stability, which contradicts known diamagnetic materials like superconductors. The resolution involves recognizing that the conjugate variables are actually the applied field H and the magnetic induction B, rather than H and magnetization M. By incorporating Faraday's law and Ampere's law to correctly calculate the work done, the theory is adjusted so that thermodynamic stability holds for both positive and negative susceptibilities.

questions.question: How do the mathematical conditions derived from maximizing total entropy for isolated systems relate to the requirements for a system to maintain stable equilibrium when interacting with a large thermal and mechanical reservoir?
questions.referenceAnswer: The section first establishes that for two isolated systems in contact, equilibrium occurs when pressure and temperature are equalized, which corresponds to a maximum in the total entropy. It then transitions to analyzing stability by requiring this entropy maximum to be global, meaning the entropy must be a concave function of its variables. Finally, these conditions are extended to a small system coupled to a large reservoir using the Gibbs potential, where stability is ensured if the second derivatives of energy with respect to entropy and volume satisfy specific inequalities that prevent spontaneous fluctuations from driving the system away from equilibrium.

questions.question: How do the definitions of state functions like internal energy contrast with heat and work in the context of reversible versus irreversible processes?
questions.referenceAnswer: The first law partitions a system's energy change into heat and work, where only the difference between these two quantities depends on the initial and final states, making internal energy a state function. In contrast, heat and work themselves are path-dependent, meaning their individual values depend on how the process occurs. This distinction is critical when comparing reversible processes, which follow a specific path in thermodynamic space that can be exactly reversed, to irreversible processes like free expansion, which do not.
goldText:
Consider a system whose state can be specified by the values of a set of state variables Xj (e.g., the volume, the number of moles of the different constituents, the magnetization, the electric polarization, etc.) and the temperature. As mentioned earlier, thermodynamics exploits an analogy with mechanics and we write, for the work done during an infinitesimal process,

where the Xj's can be thought of as generalized forces and the Xj's as generalized displacements.

The first law of thermodynamics restates the law of conservation of energy. However, it also partitions the change in energy of a system into two pieces, heat and work:

[formula]

In (1.5) dE is the change in internal energy of the system, dQ the amount of heat added to the system, and dW the amount of work done by the system during an infinitesimal process 1 . Aside from the partitioning of the energy into two parts, the formula distinguishes between the infinitesimals dE and dQ, dW. The difference between the two measurable quantities dQ and dW is found to be the same for any process in which the system evolves between two given states, independently of the path. This indicates that dE is an exact differential or, equivalently, that the internal energy is a state function. The same is not true of the differentials dQ and dW, hence the difference in notation.

Before going on to discuss the second law, we pause to introduce some terminology. A thermodynamic transformation or process is any change in the state variables of the system. A spontaneous process is one that takes place without any change in the external constraints on the system, and is due simply to the internal dynamics. An adiabatic process is one in which no heat is exchanged between the system and its surroundings. A process is isothermal if the temperature is held fixed, isobaric if the pressure is fixed, isochoric if the density is constant, and quasistatic if the process is infinitely slow. A reversible process is by nature quasistatic and follows a path in thermodynamic space which can be exactly reversed. If this is not possible, the process is irreversible. An example of a reversible process is the slow adiabatic expansion of a gas against a piston on which a force is exerted externally. This force is infmitesimally less than PA, where P is the pressure of the gas and A the area of the piston. An example of an irreversible process is the free adiabatic expansion of a gas into a vacuum. In this case the initial state of the gas can be recovered if one compresses it and removes excess heat. This is, however, not the same thermodynamic path.

1 The sign convention for the work term is not universally accepted, some authors consider work to be positive if done on the system.
